assertions.text: Output contains a @TableTest annotation
Email validation and name-required error scenarios are present — at least one row for invalid email and one for missing name.
Dietary requirements and/or accessibility needs use blank cells (null) when not provided — not 'N/A' or 'none'. These are genuinely optional and absent.

When testing pricing rules, irrelevant inputs (e.g. dietary requirements don't affect price) use value sets or representative values — not blanks (which mean null). Blanks are reserved for genuinely absent/null inputs.
Table has a scenario/description column as the leftmost column
At least one output column name ends with '?' (e.g. 'Result?', 'Price?')
Column names use domain/business language (e.g. 'Name', 'Email', 'Registration date', 'Group size', 'Price?') — not code identifiers.
Scenario names describe conditions ('Early-bird single attendee', 'Missing name') — not outcomes ('Rejected', '20% off').
Test method body contains no if or switch statements
Annotations appear in order: @DisplayName (if present), @Description (if present), @TableTest — not any other order.
Test method has either a @DisplayName annotation or a method name that reads as a clear, descriptive title when converted from camelCase/snake_case.
If @Description is present and the text is longer than a single short line, it uses a text block (triple-quoted string """), not string concatenation with +. Passes if @Description is absent.

Multiple tables (or @TableTest methods) are used, each addressing a distinct concern — not one monolithic table mixing unrelated rules. Acceptable to use a single table only when the domain genuinely has a single concern.
Each table has only the rows needed to express its concern's rules — no unnecessary permutations from combining concerns. Fewer rows per table is expected when concerns are properly separated.
Input validation and pricing/discount calculation are in separate @TableTest methods
Validation @TableTest includes Dietary Requirements and Accessibility Needs columns, with rows showing both null (blank) and non-null values are accepted — not hardcoded as null in the method body.

Registration date uses descriptive values (e.g. 'before cutoff', 'on cutoff', 'after cutoff') with a @TypeConverter method converting to actual dates — not raw date literals like '2025-02-28'. Readability over precision.

If registration dates are literal (e.g. '2025-02-28' instead of descriptive), the early-bird cutoff date appears as a separate policy column so the reader can see both dates and verify the comparison. Passes automatically if descriptive date values are used.

If @Description is present, it does not include information that is already visible in the table columns or that can be derived from the table structure — such as fixed input values that could be columns, or restating the discount rules that the rows already demonstrate.

Output column is 'Discount?' (percentage or amount off) rather than 'Price?' — making verification simpler (discount is the rule's direct output; price requires knowing the base price). If 'Price?' is used instead, both 'Base price' and 'Price?' columns must be present so the reader can trace the calculation.

Each @TableTest method has a single, uniform assertion pattern applied to all rows — not different assertions per scenario. Validation checks one thing (e.g. error message or acceptance status); pricing checks one thing (e.g. discount or price). No if/switch in assertion logic.
